newsitem.title: DUBAI: Oman aluminium smelter to go ahead without Kaiser.
newsitem.headline: Oman aluminium smelter to go ahead without Kaiser.

text.p: Plans to set up one of the Middle East's largest aluminium smelters in Oman by 2002 are on track, but are going ahead without one U.S. partner and still require final commitments from the Muscat government.
Industry executives in the region told Reuters the plan was to build a 480,000 tonne capacity smelter by about 2002 in Sohar, northern Oman, at a cost of over $2.4 billion.

They said Kaiser Aluminium Corp was no longer involved in the plans, which were put forward by a group of companies including New York-based Charus Enterprises, British generator National Power and China Non-Ferrous Metals.

"Kaiser Aluminium is no longer involved. The group is speaking to several other aluminium producers to provide the technical support," one industry source said, but declined to name potential partners.
Central to the development of the smelter is a guaranteed supply of gas for power and well-developed supporting infrastructure, including a fully fledged industrial port.
"The partners have been receiving the support of the government, which is integral to the development of Sohar," an industry executive said.
Sohar, about 200 km north of the capital Muscat, has been earmarked to be developed as a major industrial centre. At the moment its industrial zone is home to only around 20 small factories.
"We have to be sure of certain levels of support. Hopefully full government commitments will be finalised by September," the executive said.
To have the smelter running by 2002, work would have to begin by the middle to end of next year, industry sources said.

Apart from the smelter, there are also plans to develop a petrochemical plant at Sohar with BP Chemicals. Both fall within Oman's programme to diversify its economy away from dependence on the 900,000 barrels of oil it pumps daily.

A British Petroleum spokesman in London said on Wednesday BP expects to complete in September a feasibility study on the planned $900 million plant to produce 450,000 tonnes a year of ethylene and polyethelene.
Power for smelting is one of the biggest costs of aluminium production, making the gas-rich Gulf a competitive producer even though most raw materials have to be imported.
So far there are only two aluminium smelters in the region -- the 500,000 tonne annual capacity Aluminium Bahrain and the 375,000 tonne Dubai Aluminium.
